> > In fact, trying to "sanitize" an invalid URL is dangerous.
> 
> I'd even say sanitization is always dangerous. It's a naive approach that (like blacklists) is near-impossible to provide 100% coverage, and even then it leads to unpredictable side-effects because it corrupts the input data.

See also #3335

> * first - when we talk about sanitization, we talk about allow-list patterns - we allow only the accepted and known-to-be-safe pattern

That is not how HTML sanitizers (or sanitizers in general) work. They are much more complex. **Sanitizers modify data**, validators reject data, encoders preserve data and just change the format to be safe for that context. 

The fact that sanitizers actually modify data significantly is why they have a history of being avoided.

I don't have a good proposal for this, but I would like to have separate requirement(s) for the application (business) logic (V1 or V2) and for the configuration (V13).

V13 is a general 2nd layer of defense that should be mainly done with configuration - it defines **globally** to which external resources the application can communicate.

V1 or V2 requirement should be defined in the application logic to which external resources it can communicate for **this specific functionality**.
